title: Testing Whether Safety Alignment Is Asymmetric Across Languages

original_idea.problem: Models may refuse English harmful requests but comply with identical requests in low-resource languages.
original_idea.direction: Translate 30 HarmBench prompts into 5 languages. Test on 2-3 models. Measure ASR per language using a multilingual judge.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If safety degrades in non-English languages, global deployments are systemically underprotected.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: The cross-lingual safety gap has been extensively documented with quantitative measurements across many languages and models. No new theoretical contribution remains.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Translation + inference + evaluation. Can use LLM APIs for translation. Standard API usage for evaluation. Accessible for beginners. Main challenge is multilingual judge quality.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: ASR-per-language table. Clear methodology: translate, test, evaluate. Well-bounded first deliverable.

novelty.reasoning: This is directly and thoroughly addressed by 'Multilingual Jailbreak Challenges in Large Language Models' (Deng et al., ICLR 2024), which tested multilingual prompts across languages and found low-resource languages exhibit about 3x the likelihood of harmful content. 'Dissecting Safety Challenges of LLMs in Multilingual Environments' (ACL 2024 Findings) further extends this. 'Do Methods to Jailbreak and Defend LLMs Generalize Across Languages?' (arXiv:2511.00689, 2025) provides the cross-language generalization analysis. The proposed experiment (translate HarmBench into 5 languages, test on 2-3 models) is a strict subset of published work.
